    <id>https://jbrr.dev/the-american-kill-line/</id>
    <title>The American Kill Line</title>
    <updated>2026-04-25T04:59:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>jbrr</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;It's an interesting feeling to realize you've been propagandized to for your entire life. I'm simultaneously angry at those who've lied to me, although they're often victims of the same propaganda. I also feel free, and able to reanalyze all these things I thought I knew with an entirely new context for understanding the world.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I stumbled across an article from the Global Times titled “&lt;a href='https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202512/1351475.shtml'&gt;Phrase ‘US kill line’ sparks debate on American ordinary people’s economic fragility and social safety nets on Chinese social media&lt;/a&gt;."
The Global Times is explicitly Chinese state media, so take it for what it is, and be aware of it's bias.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The article explains that "kill line" is zoomer slang referring to when you're playing a game, and your health is low enough that you can be killed with one shot (apparently, idk, I've never heard it, but I'm not a gamer). The gist of the article is that Chinese kids are starting to learn about American poverty, and about how close so many Americans are to being homeless, and they don't have a way to relate to it. In 1979, the Chinese government made a goal of creating a "moderately prosperous society." That is, a society made up almost entirely of the middle class, with no extremes at either end. It was an ambitious goal, as the World Bank estimated that 88% of the population of China lived in extreme poverty. Over the last forty years, they've managed to bring 850,000,000 people out of poverty by devoting their economy to centrally planned jobs programs similar to The New Deal in the United States. It's an absolutely staggering accomplishment, and they're not done yet, but the progress they've made is nothing short of miraculous. It's remarkable what can happen when government focuses it's spending internally, on it's own citizens.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The idea that all Americans know that we're just a few bad dice rolls away from complete financial ruin, and that we all more-or-less accept it, is absolutely wild. It struck me recently that last year was without a doubt the most devastating year of my life, and if I didn't have family that could support me financially, and didn't get extremely lucky at work, there's a good chance I'd have lost everything as a result.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/eioua/342758408"&gt;&lt;figure style="display: inline-block; width: 100%; text-align: center; margin: 0;"&gt;
&lt;img 
        src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/jbrr/342758408_c286e56d4e_c.webp" 
        alt="Train at dawn taken on a disposable camera" 
        style="max-width: 70%; margin: 0 auto;"
    /&gt;
&lt;figcaption&gt;
&lt;i&gt;Slow Train Comin'&lt;/i&gt;
&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To set the stage, I was unemployed for about 10 months in 2024. I lost my job in March, and didn't start a new one until December. So I came into the year with considerable debt just from trying to make it through 2024. Then, of course, my wife died in early February. It was impossible to give a shit about literally anything else for months (which I still struggle with now, 15 months out). I'm extraordinarily lucky that my brand new job gave me basically as much time as I needed. I had only been there for two months, after all, they didn't owe me anything. Even so, I don't like that people need to get lucky to make it through situations like that, as opposed to having a publicly funded safety net that we could count on.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then, in May my gall bladder decided to get infected, and once again, had I not gotten lucky with how supportive my work was and if I didn't have health insurance at the time, it could've single handedly put me underwater. The hospital bill was something like $60,000 without insurance. If all that hadn't managed to wipe me out, a microburst of wind in my back yard sending an entire whole-ass tree falling on top of my house might've. There's a possible world in which I'm homeless right now.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I've realized that people don't hate homeless people for any particular reason (and no doubt about it, housed people &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; hate the homeless, although they rarely come out and say it). People hate homeless people because they're a reminder of exactly how close 95% of Americans are to the same fate. Instead of blaming the systems that allow homelessness to happen in the first place, we've been propagandized into blaming the homeless people themselves.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But it doesn't have to be this way. There are better ways to organize a country and economy, we know that for an absolute fact. China's done it. Do you know how much it would cost to permanently house all of the homeless people in the entire country? &lt;a href='https://endhomelessness.org/resources/research-and-analysis/how-much-would-it-cost-to-provide-housing-first-to-all-households-staying-in-homeless-shelters/'&gt;Roughly $9.6 billion&lt;/a&gt;. Put another way, it would cost &lt;a href='https://www.warcosts.org/analysis/iran-war-cost-breakdown'&gt;about five days of this war we started in Iran&lt;/a&gt; for no particular reason. That's just the military spend. The devastation that this war will continue to wreck on the economy makes the two costs almost non-comparable.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Is China a utopia where everyone has everything they need? Of course not. Do they have their issues with human rights and censorship? Of course. And naturally, that's all &lt;a href='https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/13/business/china-american-poverty.html?unlocked_article_code=1.dlA.LdSv.Ze3QredV9gAk&amp;smid=url-share'&gt;the New York Times boiled down the whole "American Kill Line" concept to&lt;/a&gt; - Chinese propaganda, nothing more. But it seems obvious to me that they're doing something right.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Today, Meta and Nike announced new rounds of layoffs, and Microsoft announced they'd be offering early retirement to people (and presumably laying people off if the offers aren't taken). Amazon laid off 30,000 people already this year (but don't worry, &lt;a href='https://www.techspot.com/news/112028-amazon-laid-off-30000-workers-while-ceo-andy.html'&gt;the CEO got a 30% raise and stock is up 14.67% since the start of the year&lt;/a&gt;). Block and Salesforce have also announced massive layoffs, and have explicitly blamed it on AI reducing their need for human employees. And of course, because of last year's Big Beautiful Bill, all of these tech industry workers being laid off won't be able to get on Medicaid, and because of the war and tarriffs, inflation is skyrocketing and &lt;em&gt;everything&lt;/em&gt; is more expensive.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Our economy is broken. We need to try something new, and we need to try it soon, because the amount of people suffering has been rising drastically over the past 10 years, and it's going to continue to rise as wealth inequality reaches new extremes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;We have a rare chance these midterm elections to elect representatives who are about as far left as Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Ilhan Omar. People absolutely hate Trump and the Republican run congress. Yet somehow, people hate the Democrats almost as much! It's remarkable. But it leaves the door open for Democratic challengers from the left who want to implement real, drastic change. In Denver, &lt;a href='https://www.kirosforco.com/'&gt;Melat Kiros&lt;/a&gt; is launching a strong primary campaign against Diana Degette, our 14-term congresswoman. In Michigan, Dr. Abdul Sayed is running a strong primary for the Democratic nomination for the Senate. There are examples of this all over the country, of socialists and leftists running for office. I don't know about you, but I've seen enough of where imperialist neoliberal policies get us, and I'm ready to try something new.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://vics.me/teacher-slop/</id>
    <title>the teacher who groomed me in high school is posting ai slop on youtube now</title>
    <updated>2026-04-25T01:30:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>vics</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;i have google alerts set up for my high school and its associated creeps. this guy’s name was a jump scare in my email this morning.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;when i thought i knew him, he was pursuing an arts-related phd and was the smartest, most interesting person i’d ever met. he traveled internationally to present at conferences, which sounded important, and lectured as if building up to an &lt;em&gt;o captain! my captain!&lt;/em&gt; ovation from students.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;for over a decade, our relationship lived in my head as a largely impotent schoolgirl crush – i was enamored and he indulged, but only a little bit, and only for a moment.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;a few years after graduation, a friend visited me at college and yelled in my ear over the bass at an outdoor club: “you know what he did was fucked up though, right?”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;between pestering me for suggestive photos and inviting me to “say something sexy, say something scandalous, say something provocative,” he found time to nurture my love of writing and budding interest in feminism.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;he introduced me to artists like carolee schneemann and marina ambromovic, to bell hooks and audre lorde. he gave me access to his jstor account and printed a dozen articles for me to read about the body as art or medium or whatever. he would send me excerpts from his dissertation and i would vague-post poetry about him online, which he would respond to via text.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;we spent hours “synthesizing” my “research” into a cohesive “narrative” “portfolio” for my application to his undergrad alma mater; his feedback was signed “your biggest fan” in big, curly letters. when i was accepted into the program, we cried and embraced dramatically in front of my classmates. and when i was in the fitting room trying on junior prom dresses, he told me he wanted to see.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;it’s impossible for these vignettes to coexist in my mind – the image of him pouring life into me and the one of him teasing it out – and so, over time, both gave way to a new memory, where i was the one goading and coaxing and prodding and he humored me to avoid hurting my fragile, teenage feelings, which is still bad, but in a way that insists he was just a little drunk on his own koolaid and not the alternative.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;the best parts of me, i knew, came from him, and my stomach burned with betrayal when i considered anything else.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;then, in my late-twenties, our school was in the news for a similar story involving another teacher and i started having panic attacks when driving in its direction on my visits home.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;it was a visceral repulsion, as if the big atrium of the main building had a miles-wide blast radius i couldn’t breach.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;the relationship was secretive, but not subtle. we ate lunch together in his office daily, sometimes in coordinating outfits if he texted me that morning with instructions for what to wear.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;our “work” was often in dark rooms during skipped class periods, or in the hours between school and some monthly fundraising obligation i was eager to volunteer for because i could, like, you know, just stay here instead of going home and coming back later, if that’s okay with you.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;it was always okay with him.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i’m still not clear on what was my idea and what was his – whether i was the one who asked to go for coffee, whether he was the one who offered to pick me up.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;another year and the disorientation became overwhelming.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;when you are hiding something from yourself – protecting yourself from it – you feel fractured: one part of you braced against the door and another part of you slamming into it from the other side. you want to believe it’s for your own good, but you know that it isn’t, you know that opening this door is your one task of this moment.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;so i eventually pulled the two peeling pleather journals off the shelf, the ones where i’d written this story out in real time, the ones i had refused to read because i already knew what happened and i didn’t need to go looking because what was there to find.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i bargained with myself that i could flip to a single random page, and if i didn’t see anything weird, i had to admit defeat and for the love of god move on with my life.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;except i did see something weird.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;obviously.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;the next week was effectively spent in a k-hole of my own past trying to understand how i didn’t remember literally any of this. it’s like i was retroactively violating myself reading back through such meticulous records and transcribed texts – comments about the size of my body, a story of him spamming messages about my perfume during class and watching for my reaction, the way he punished me with silence when i wouldn’t take the bait to escalate our relationship further.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;it wasn’t just him, or this, but two brutal years of my life that had been neutered in my memory. i stared at the wall for hours trying to square what i was reading with what i was sure i thought i knew.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;this shattering of your perspective feels physical. your vision goes blurry and it’s as if you’re floating in some liminal space, because your through-line has snapped and suddenly your journey from there to here doesn’t make sense anymore and where is here anyway? you don’t know because you don’t know anything.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;/&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;anyway, looks like he started a new youtube channel. curiosity got the best of me and i found myself watching an ai-generated version of him in an ai-generated boardroom, his ai-generated voice reading some ai-generated script about being hungry for hard work or something.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i scrolled more and had to stop when i heard, “what’s up, guys!” in, to his credit, the most youtube voice i’ve ever heard.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;his websites, too, are full of blog posts and media analyses written by chatgpt, and not even a good model.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;which is all to say:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i guess the rest of the illusion broke. whoever i thought he was would hate him.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:hi@vics.me"&gt;reply via email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://shewrites.bearblog.dev/cognitive-surrender/</id>
    <title>Cognitive Surrender</title>
    <updated>2026-04-25T01:20:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>shewrites</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I've marveled lately at the active surrendering of cognition to AI that I've witnessed.&lt;br /&gt;
I watched a guy at work use ChatGPT to draft a four-sentence letter for a customer. I said "that's ridiculous, man" and he said "it just helps me sound better" which didn't make it less ridiculous to me. He's fully capable of drafting that letter on his own in just a couple minutes if he wanted to. It would have sounded perfectly fine. I've seen him perform similar tasks, and I'm 100% certain he could have done it. But instead, he let AI do it for him because it was faster and easier. There wasn't any rush. He just didn't want to &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; the thinking.&lt;br /&gt;
The same guy was paying for a monthly subscription to ChatGPT for a while (canceled it now, though), and has used it to tell him if his outfit looked good. 'Cause who cares what &lt;em&gt;he&lt;/em&gt; thinks of his outfit, right? Better get AI to give him an "opinion" so he knows he doesn't look like a fool. It genuinely blows my mind. I don't care what another &lt;em&gt;person&lt;/em&gt; thinks of my outfit, let alone a fucking AI model.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I get angry about this sort of thing. Part of that anger has to do with the environmental disregard, and the lack of empathy for communities already impacted by data center pollution. But I think it's also a fear response. I get mad because the world I see developing in front of me is scary. It could still be stopped. We don't &lt;em&gt;have&lt;/em&gt; to forfeit our minds to the computers. I know AI isn't going anywhere, but we don't have to surrender the very thing that makes us human to it either. AI isn't capable of cognition. It has superior computing power, and has been trained on far more expansive materials. But &lt;em&gt;we&lt;/em&gt; are the dominant beings. Will we always be, though? Or are we staring down the barrel of a bad sci-fi movie where all the main characters make the dumbest fucking decisions and sacrifice our species in the process?&lt;br /&gt;
We'll have to protect our daughter from AI proliferation and cognitive surrender. Her generation is the first to grow up without knowing a world before AI was in everything. It scares me that we might not be able to protect her&amp;mdash;that pressure from the world around her when she's not safe in my arms might overpower our parenting. But I suppose all I can do is my damndest. As with everything, I think, it starts with the example.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I laugh or shake my head sometimes at the old folks who are so resistant to well-established technology like debit cards, online banking, and email. That's probably going to be me some day when it comes to AI. But at least I won't be one who surrendered my mind to it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h5 id=a-hrefmailtoshewritesonbearprotonmereply-via-emaila&gt;&lt;a href='mailto:shewritesonbear@proton.me'&gt;Reply via email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h5&gt;</content>
    <link href="https://shewrites.bearblog.dev/cognitive-surrender/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-25T01:20:00+00:00</published>

  <entry>
    <id>https://untangled.bearblog.dev/bye-substack/</id>
    <title>Bye, Substack.</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T15:14:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>untangled</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I quit Instagram in October 2025.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It’s been a weird and winding road getting here (and honestly the last six months have been weird to begin with, a story for another day), but I finally feel like I’ve found a virtual home.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When I quit Insta and Booksta, I had the best intentions. The plan was to go all in on my Ghost site, tell my friends on Instagram that I’d be writing my book reviews over there and they can get them right in their email inbox. It was great.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Until it wasn’t.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It was quite lonely, actually. Ghost didn’t have great discoverability, though I know they’re working on it. &lt;em&gt;Me and my 8 subscribers against the world.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In November, money got tight. So paying for Ghost was unfortunately out of the question. I began looking for alternatives, not really sure what I was looking for (except that it had to be free, because every penny counted).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Seeing how easy discoverability was on Substack, I was sold. I announced that I was moving, pulled my little list over to Substack, and started building what I thought would be my new home there.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There’s something… addictive about Substack, though. I was spending a lot of time on the app, but I wasn’t writing. I was scrolling Notes, subscribing and following tons of new people (&lt;em&gt;who I eventually had to unsubscribe from, because the number of emails I was getting was ridiculous&lt;/em&gt;). I was getting the same dopamine hits that I was trying to escape from on Instagram.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I was also inundated with messaging that encouraged me to “monetize”, to scale, to grow my newsletter. There are &lt;em&gt;so many&lt;/em&gt; great writers over there and the pressure to write something AMAZING that also got you paid subscribers and picked up on Notes was just… a lot. I often didn’t write at all because it didn’t feel like I had anything important to contribute. Nothing important enough to get someone to pay me. Imposter syndrome followed me like a shadow.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It was around January or February 2026 when I found Bear.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And it feels like coming up for air, honestly. I’m aging myself here, but I remember early internet days fiddling with html and css on chat forums like InvisionFree, MyBB, Myspace and Neopets. 20+ years ago, the internet was like the wild west. And that’s the vibe I get from Bear and the blogs around here. Little virtual playgrounds where you can just do what you want and really make it your own. I’m hearing a ton about &lt;a href='https://indieweb.org/' target='_blank'&gt;Indie Web&lt;/a&gt; lately and I’m ready to fully step into it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So, here I am. I pulled over a few of my favorite pieces of recent writing and now I’m on to new stuff.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Bye, Substack. Hello, Bear.
Thanks for giving me a place to land.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="reply-email"&gt;

&lt;/div&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://guinevak.bearblog.dev/well-if-youd-just/</id>
    <title>Well if you'd just</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T21:37:56.693959+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>guinevak</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I am simply and passionately Done with people telling other people that what they do to survive is unethical.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The argument is always based in "alternatives" that not everyone has.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;"Just eat plant-based foods:" because those are freely and cheaply available everywhere? Because grain, fruit, and vegetable farming isn't exploitative of sentient beings or the environment? Because you can overcome your allergies and aversions if you care enough about cows?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;"Just get a better job:" because jobs that pay a living wage are just lying around for the taking? Because being trafficked is a choice? Because things like "eating" and "not dying of exposure" can wait until you convince someone to pay you for something you're not ashamed to do?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;"Just don't give money to--" yeah, okay, sure. A handful of vast conglomerates own &lt;em&gt;everything on earth&lt;/em&gt;. Even if you can live naked in a field eating nothing but organic native grasses (which, more power to you), you're still going to have to pay taxes to a corrupt government.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;"No ethical consumption under capitalism" isn't an &lt;em&gt;excuse&lt;/em&gt;. It's a fact. Everyone alive on this planet has to make moral compromises in order to live at all. Yes, some of those compromises are more defensible than others. That doesn't mean you get to tell strangers on the internet that they're bad people because they want to survive in a shitty world.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Am I saying you can't talk shit about internet strangers at all? Of course not. Things that are not crucial to anyone's survival include but are not limited to: inflicting pain for shits and giggles! Getting ChatGPT to write your term papers! Calling abuse survivors liars! Shitting in someone's Cheerios! Driving 90mph on a one-lane road at 3 am! Playing your music so loudly that the neighbor's house shakes! Arbitrarily declaring people subhuman based on their physical characteristics! Making your child feel bad about their weight! Travelling around the world for the sole purpose of killing large animals so you can prove your dominance! Wearing your underpants on your head! Cheering for someone's death! Leaving the toilet seat up! There are &lt;em&gt;any number&lt;/em&gt; of reasons -- valid, invalid, profound, petty -- to criticize other people's behavior.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But "they're doing whatever they have to in order to live any kind of life" is not on the list.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://guinevak.bearblog.dev/well-if-youd-just/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-24T21:37:56.693959+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/hayao-miyazaki-and-optimistic-nihilism/</id>
    <title>Hayao Miyazaki and optimistic nihilism</title>
    <updated>2026-04-25T14:55:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>pinewind</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Yesterday, I found a post &lt;a href='https://sheilz.bearblog.dev/whimsy/' target='_blank'&gt;i think we're obsessed with aesthetic&lt;/a&gt; on the Discovery Feed. It featured quite a few nice quotes. My favourite was this one:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="picwcap" style="margin-bottom: 1rem;"&gt;
&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/sheilz/download-14.webp" alt="A set of two cuts from a documentary showing Hayao Miyazaki, looking at a sunset and saying: It really is beautiful. When you die, you can't see sunsets."&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It's a real &lt;a href='https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q3U_gGimekg' target='_blank'&gt;"people die when they are killed"&lt;/a&gt; kind of quote. Your first reaction is probably going to be some faint amusement, accompanied by a thought like &lt;em&gt;Well, duh. Thanks, Captain Obvious.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; But aside from the &lt;em&gt;factual&lt;/em&gt; layer, it also has a personal, contemplative element. This scene shows one of those moments where you see something that you've seen a thousand times and suddenly feel a deep sense of appreciation. You come from non-existence, and go back into it. The time where you get to experience sunsets or soothing spring rain or beautiful autumn leaves is just a tiny fraction of existence as a whole. From that perspective, even the most commonplace, mundane or tacky things can seem truly beautiful.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think this scene is from the documentary "The Kingdom of Dreams and Madness", which has circulated pretty widely online. I've never actually seen the whole thing, just the clips of it that get uploaded on YouTube. Another one I like is &lt;a href='https://youtu.be/eED1ALOtaYw?si=E4TzPooluqmObAle&amp;t=75' target='_blank'&gt;this one&lt;/a&gt;. The interviewer asks: "Aren't you worried about the studio's future?"&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Miyazaki's response:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;The future is clear. It's going to fall apart. [laughs] I can already see it. What's the use worrying? It's inevitable. [...] "Ghibli" is just a random name that I got from an airplane. It's only a name.&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;He then walks away, and the interviewer quietly says "how beautiful", to herself. I find that last part ruins the scene a bit; it feels like the interviewer is telling the audience how to interpret what was just said. It would've been much more effective to just end with the shot of Miyazaki walking across the garden.&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-2"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-2"&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; However, a short scroll through the comments under the video will tell you that people still have different opinions on Miyazaki's stance. Some criticise him for being a stubborn old fart who'd rather let his studio fall apart than properly train a successor and make sure it continues to live on. Others just see him as a bitter nihilist.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To me, these quotes embody a kind of &lt;em&gt;optimistic nihilism.&lt;/em&gt; Yes, nothing is forever. Everything will return to nothing one day; the world and our lives don't have inherent meaning. But despite of that, or rather &lt;em&gt;precisely because&lt;/em&gt; of that, it becomes meaningful what you do with your life, and how you choose to live it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Miyazaki's oeuvre makes it obvious that he's not a bitter defeatist who declared life to be meaningless and simply gave up. Quite the contrary, he's dedicated his life to art and creativity, with all the self-discipline, self-criticism, doubt and despair that comes with it. He's a "suffering artist" type, but not one that wallows in their suffering or sees it as the &lt;em&gt;source&lt;/em&gt; of their art. He simply accepts it as a consequence of life.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When he laughs after saying that the studio is going to fall apart, it's not a laugh of self-pity, or a mask for disillusionment. It's a laugh born out of the awareness that all things will eventually fade away, and that, from a "cosmic" perspective, all human efforts are but small scratches on the ground. This serves as a way to balance out the deep attachment he has to his work. It's an &lt;a href='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absurdism' target='_blank'&gt;Absurdist&lt;/a&gt; take, really. The same is true for the comment about the name of the studio. It's just that, a random name, an empty container, like a drinking glass. The glass is only a vehicle for the water, tea, or juice you fill it with. At the same time, it's what &lt;em&gt;allows&lt;/em&gt; you to drink the water, tea, or juice - meaningless and meaningful at the same time.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Some of the comments under the YouTube video point out that the end of the movie &lt;em&gt;The Boy and the Heron&lt;/em&gt; represents Miyazaki truly coming to terms with the things that he says in this interview, or maybe truly internalising their meaning. Instead of desperately trying to hold onto a form (the Studio) and trying to find a successor, he realises (and posits to us, via the movie) that it's not the form that matters, but the spirit. It doesn't matter whether or not people use &lt;em&gt;your&lt;/em&gt; drinking glass - treating it as some kind of heirloom, or letting it shatter on the ground. As long as they too realise the value of drinking a cold lemonade on a summer evening or hot tea during a cold winter, &lt;em&gt;any&lt;/em&gt; glass, cup or mug will do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unless you believe in some kind of afterlife where you get to enjoy sunsets for the rest of eternity.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-2"&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a documentary, so it's obviously "staged" to some degree. I don't believe that Miyazaki is lying, or the interviewer is simply reading off a script with her response. Still, the context that allowed these images to get end up guiding them in a certain direction, another kind of inevitability.&lt;a href="#fnref-2" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/hayao-miyazaki-and-optimistic-nihilism/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-25T14:55:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://blog.absurdpirate.com/break-stupid-rules/</id>
    <title>Break Stupid Rules</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T16:20:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>absurdpirate</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;This one may be a controversial one, but I'm writing it anyway.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You've heard the saying "rules are meant to be broken", for the most part I agree. Some "rules" are basically just common sense, or what should be common sense: don't dive on the shallow end of the pool, don't light a match near a gas tank, clip your nails before entry, stuff like that.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;However some rules are just... stupid. Pointless even. Existing only for the sake of seemingly keeping people in line. This is done either socially or legally. Many self-imposed rules exist simply because they have "always been done that way". Many legal rules aren't even enforceable.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=why-should-i-break-rules&gt;Why should I break rules?&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Little acts of defiance in the face of the authority that insists upon its own legitimacy go a long way for when it comes time to do something for the greater good. The civil rights movement was built upon breaking laws, black people sitting in a whites-only restaurant was illegal. Breaking the small stuff makes it easier for when it comes time to break the big stuff.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You also start to exercise why certain rules became rules, like the aforementioned don't dive head-first into the shallow end of the pool. The rule is in-place for your safety, but the rule isn't enforceable. It just becomes a guideline or boundary.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Another byproduct of breaking small arbitrary rules is it becomes easier to not fall victim into herd mentality. You've basically trained that "muscle" in your brain to ignore the scoffs and the social anxiety. You begin to recognize your own autonomy as a person.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You may also spark within someone that confidence to follow suit and maybe start questioning what is just social conditioning vs something actually meant for personal/social safety.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;"In order to liberate others, one must liberate themselves", as the saying goes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=what-rules-should-i-break&gt;What rules should I break?&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;I really can't answer this for you. It's up to you and understanding your own agency in deciding what personal social/legal rules you want to break.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But a simple starting-out rule that I often tell people they can break first is social/work-related ones. Low stakes. Here's some examples:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When someone asks you "how are you doing?", don't default to "good, you?". Be a bit more open, doesn't have to give deep details, you can just say something like "Honestly, pretty tired." or "pretty great, got a little love note from my wife this morning with breakfast while I was heading out the door" (this one I used recently). You can also make some joke to break the monotony, I like saying "Awake and not crying" which often gets a chuckle.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Wear pajamas when going to the grocery store or alternatively overdress when going to the grocery store. We often always say we'll wear X fancy thing on a special occasion. You're alive, that is a special occasion, wear that dress.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Be honest without being a dick when someone asks for your opinion. Work on shedding that fear of expressing your opinion. If you're in school, raise your hand to answer questions if you otherwise don't out of fear of looking "stupid", you're in school you're all relatively stupid. If you feel the urge to be productive, fight that urge and try to give yourself a break, you don't need to productive at all times. For men, do/wear something that someone else might call "gay" or "feminine". So on and so on.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I can go on listing a bunch of examples, but then this blog would be a fucking novel. This is just a way to spark ideas for what is supposed to act as a sort of "gateway drug" to the "harder stuff"&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=the-harder-stuff&gt;The Harder Stuff&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now you're breaking real rules. Yesterday's telling someone you don't feel like going to some gathering instead of trying to make up an excuse, is today's jaywalking.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Now for the harder stuff. These ones might take a bit more courage to do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;For me, it's been at my train stations. For context, there's platforms you stand at to board the train, and a ramp that leads to a walkway that you're supposed to use to cross to the other platforms. I started just jumping down and jumping back up onto the platform, completely skipping the long walk around down the ramp. I'm physically capable of doing so, the rails aren't electrified, and the train doesn't move nearly fast enough to catch me by surprise (it barely goes above 20mph when approaching a station).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Another example is Jaywalking. If there is literally no cars anywhere in sight, just walk across. People will often follow with you to my surprise. Some might not, some might give you an odd look. Good. You're doing multiple things, stress testing your reflex to obey, as well as combatting that peer pressure. For me, it's also one small act of defying the car-centric society and infrastructure we've built.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You have to be aware of your surroundings with these ones. Be aware of any potential immediate threats, cars, trains, bikes, cops. The idea is to stress test, not land yourself with a medical bill or a ticket.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After seeing a video of traffic in the Netherlands where people were walking, biking, and driving without any form of stop sign/light in sight. I obviously wouldn't jump down if there was an active train coming (look both ways and all that). I started questioning "what's stopping us from doing this for ourselves?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There's also dealing with confrontation. Telling some pervert harassing someone to pound sand for example. Or putting a racist in his place. An example that I think about often is this time my wife and I were on a bus waiting to get back to the cruise ship while on a stop in Mexico. There was this couple, a Thai woman I had a conversation with and this dollar store Henry Winkler looking motherfucker she unfortunately calls a husband. In the front of the bus came this group of Chinese women who were talking amongst themselves in Mandarin. Well, old coot decided to start loudly shouting that stereotypical "bing bong ching chong" shit that racists do to make fun of Asian people. Made my fucking blood boil, but I did nothing in that moment out of the likelihood of escalation. I'm not afraid of confrontation. I've worked in retail and have told customers in no uncertain terms to kiss my ass, but in the moment I didn't. Maybe had my wife not been there, who is far more anxious about confrontation than me, I would have. Anyway, He eventually stopped when his wife got him to stop being an asshole for a second, but I regret not saying something. Never again.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Do what you feel you feasibly can safely. Commit time theft at work, tag a political message in a bathroom stall with sharpie (I mean in areas like a 7-11 or some franchise, not a small coffee shop), pirate from greedy corporations, etc., etc.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;All this to essentially be said, exercise your personal autonomy and practice sticking up for yourself/others and practice defiance in the face of oppressive systems.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=in-conclusion&gt;In conclusion&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is just one aspect of proper social change, but a very important one. Ruthlessly question the legitimacy of a social/institutional rule, and if it ends up making no sense and if you feel safe enough doing so to push yourself out of your comfort zone, then do it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If you read all this, congratulations. You just got tricked into reading a little bit about Anarchist calisthenics. If you want a little more information, I'll share &lt;a href='https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/anonymous-anarchist-calisthenics'&gt;this link&lt;/a&gt;. Even if you don't consider yourself an anarchist, it's still a useful tool because one day protests aren't going to be these neat little government-sanctioned marches on a Saturday. With that, I'll leave you with this little quote:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;“One day you will be called on to break a big law in the name of justice and rationality. Everything will depend on it. You have to be ready. How are you going to prepare for that day when it really matters? You have to stay ‘in shape’ so that when the big day comes you will be ready. What you need is ‘anarchist calisthenics.’ Every day or so break some trivial law that makes no sense, even if it’s only jaywalking. Use your own head to judge whether a law is just or reasonable. That way, you’ll keep trim; and when the big day comes, you’ll be ready.” —James C. Scott, Two Cheers For Anarchism&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a class="previous-post" href="/i-fucking-love-trains" title="I Fucking Love Trains"&gt;Previous&lt;/a&gt; | &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Reply via email: &lt;a href='mailto:me@absurdpirate.com'&gt;me@absurdpirate.com&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;h3 id=as-of-writing-this&gt;as of writing this...&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Ready for the weekend. Just wanna spend time with my family. Been making good progress on Blood Meridian finally now that I'm taking a train to commute to work. I read about 1-2 chapters each day, and when I finish a chapter I'll often just stare out the window at the view. I tried seeing if I could use my skateboard to make my walk from car-to-station-to-work faster, and about ate shit so I'm gonna have to practice (and maybe get some better wheels). Also been working on a Windows XP gaming rig which has been fun, got that aquarium screensaver going.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

    <id>https://lwgrs.bearblog.dev/my-own-bic-pen-experiment/</id>
    <title>My own BIC pen experiment</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T15:38:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>lwgrs</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Once again, shame on me for forgetting where I first found this post:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href='https://tinkerdwarf.bearblog.dev/the-bic-pen-experiment-part-3/?ref=bubbles.town'&gt;The BIC Pen Experiment, Part 3 | The Tinkering Dwarf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I know it's on &lt;a href='https://bubbles.town/entry/110702'&gt;Bubbles&lt;/a&gt; but I am fairly certain I saw it on someone else's round-up. Maybe &lt;a href="https://joelchrono.xyz/" class="nametag"&gt;Joel&lt;/a&gt;?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Anyway the gist of the experiment was to see how long it would take to use up the ink well in a classic &lt;a href='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bic_Cristal'&gt;BIC cristal pen&lt;/a&gt;. It's one of my favourite reliable pens and I don't think I'm alone in that matter. It writes well and is smooth - what more do you want from a cheap ballpoint?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have a vast collection of pens at my disposal, and in the interest of actually using all of them, I switch between pens week-to-week. Upon reading this experiment I decided to grab my &lt;a href='https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ulooMspLUok'&gt;BIC Cristal ReNew&lt;/a&gt; from my locker at work on Monday and have committed to using it up&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As of Monday it was about half-full, and as I type today, it's not far from the same spot. I don't write as much on weekends so it may take a while to empty it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h6 id=a-hrefhttpsletterbirdcosrgreply-by-emaila-nbsp-a-hrefhttpswwwaddtoanycomshareurl-post_link-title-post_title-target_blankshare-this-postanbsp-a-hrefhttpsottawaplacesrgowermastodonanbsp-a-hrefhttpsbskyappprofilesrgowercomblueskya&gt;&lt;a href="https://letterbird.co/srg"&gt;Reply by email&lt;/a&gt; &amp;nbsp; &lt;a href="https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https://lwgrs.bearblog.dev/my-own-bic-pen-experiment&amp;title=My own BIC pen experiment" target="_blank"&gt;Share this post&lt;/a&gt;&amp;nbsp; &lt;a href='https://ottawa.place/@srgower/'&gt;Mastodon&lt;/a&gt;&amp;nbsp; &lt;a href='https://bsky.app/profile/srgower.com'&gt;Bluesky&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h6&gt;&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a neat, slick-looking pen that is re-loadable! I have another ink well in my locker and if I so-chose I could put in a blue ink well from another pen. But for this time I'm just using up this ink well, I'm not going to use up &lt;em&gt;both&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;

    <id>https://diels-daydreams.bearblog.dev/what-i-like-here-in-bear/</id>
    <title>What I like here in Bear</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T00:31:50.470199+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>diels-daydreams</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I meant to write it for some time, so let’s start it well. I really like Bear.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It has been really nice and changed my perspective on a lot of things. So I decided to do a short list in no particular order about the things I like here.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;1 - The community. You guys are amazing! All the messages I have received were nothing short of pleasant. People are very willing to reach out to talk about your post and give their input. Thank you to everyone who read my posts and sent me a message or mentioned them in their own posts. I’m very grateful and honored.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;2 - Personal post. A lot of the bigger blogs here have a very neat and professional style of writing. Probably because of their background and practice. But the posts that intrigued me the most were those filled with emotion. The ones that make you feel like reading someone's diary, with messy writing, abbreviations, grammatical errors, no formatting, and pages flooded with bottled-up emotions. Those always got a grip on me.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;3 - Photos. I love photos! Sometimes I leave a toast in a post solely because of the picture. I started to post &lt;a href='https://diels-daydreams.bearblog.dev/blog/?q=Photos'&gt;some&lt;/a&gt; too, even made a &lt;a href='https://diels-daydreams.bearblog.dev/gallery/'&gt;gallery&lt;/a&gt;. Please post more pictures/photos, you can use the &lt;a href='https://robertbirming.com/bearming/add-ons/'&gt;Robert Birming&lt;/a&gt; add-on if you don’t like how it looks “raw”, he has a lot of useful stuff, I super recommend it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;4 - Emails. I like the lack of comments. Having people email me their opinions and compliments feels so much more thought out and personal. It opens margin for a private discussion, a back and forth of ideas. I appreciate it a lot more than when I used Komments in the past. (&lt;del&gt;by the way, for some reason, I got a lot of Russian comments there even with the links deactivated&lt;/del&gt;)&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So, that is it! I was not expecting to be so well received here, so I made up my mind to make an appreciation post. Thank you very much, everyone! &lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Thanks for reading! You can leave a comment &lt;a href='https://letterbird.co/dielisdaydreaming'&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;

    <id>https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/you-should-aim-to-make-fuck-you-money-respond-to-feedback/</id>
    <title>You Should Aim to Make Fuck You Money | Respond to Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T03:15:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>livingkindfully</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I received a few comments about my post on &lt;a href='https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/you-should-aim-to-make-fuck-you-money' target='_blank'&gt;"You Should Aim to Make Fuck You Money"&lt;/a&gt;. Most of the comments were about me promoting materialism and putting money ahead of everything such as family and love.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think some of my readers missed the main plot. It is my fault for not writing it clearly. Making "Fuck You" money means having the ability to say no to things that you hate. It also means knowing when to focus on doing things that you enjoy. Life is more than just making money; you know you have enough when you can say "Fuck You".&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;While a few said I am putting money ahead of family and love. Money will never be ahead of family and love. However, money enables many things and experiences. I still remember my silence and helplessness when my family asked for tuition fees. How I worry about supporting the family when I suffered &lt;a href='https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/i-just-lost-usd470436-and-i-cannot-let-my-family-know/' target='_blank'&gt;my large financial loss&lt;/a&gt;. I can't even look at myself in the mirror as I know I have failed as a provider to the family. My wife and kids are very supportive. The only way to express my gratitude and love is to give them the best life that I can afford. I cannot drag the whole family down due to my stupidity and ignorance. My "Fuck You" money is different from others. I just want to let my family to live the life that they deserve. It is never about buying things but finding opportunities to do things together.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It is fine that you do not want to make "Fuck You" money. Your priority is different. Maybe you already making "Fuck You" money that's why you can say such things. May you never need to feel "helpless" over money issues.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/you-should-aim-to-make-fuck-you-money-respond-to-feedback/" rel="alternate"/>

  <entry>
    <id>https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/focusing-on-the-process-and-casual-wabi-sabi/</id>
    <title>"focusing on the process" and casual wabi-sabi</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T13:30:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>pinewind</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Recently, while scrolling through pictures that I took on my phone last year, this one caught my eye.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="picture-wrapper"&gt;
&lt;img src="https://i.imgur.com/apKlQ0E.png" class="bigger-single" alt="Photograph of a paperback book, a coffee mug, an open sketchbook with a ballpoint pen and a white iPhone with simple earplugs wrapped around it"&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I photographed this at some kind of design exhibition. I don't remember the topic anymore, or how this exhibit tied into the exhibition as a whole. However, both back then and now, when looking at the picture again, I found this arrangement of objects to be &lt;em&gt;attractive&lt;/em&gt; somehow ... even though the individual elements aren't. The iPhone is worn around the edges, without a protective case. The book is battered and broken (the spine has been fixed with tape). The drawings in the notebook are crude, drawn with a cheap ballpoint pen. The mug looks like it belongs in a dingy 80s coffee shop.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Aside from the iPhone, the ensemble looks very &lt;em&gt;retro&lt;/em&gt;. That is definitely part of its appeal to me. But that's not all there is to it. More so than the retro-nostalgia element, what appeals to me is the &lt;em&gt;frankness&lt;/em&gt; with which these things are presented.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I don't know who these items belong to (or if they even belong to one specific person at all). However, they still evoke an image: The image of a person who is a bit messy, but tends to keep things simple. Someone who doesn't care too much if their iPhone gets scratches or their book becomes worn down. They probably know that their drawings aren't very good, but it's not really the quality they're concerned with, anyway. The drawings are just vehicles for working out something else. And to get there, they'll use their tools extensively, without worrying about appearances. It's a kind of &lt;em&gt;messy chic&lt;/em&gt;, a form of contemporary, casual &lt;em&gt;wabi-sabi.&lt;/em&gt; It gets its appeal from the implication that the person using these tools is a &lt;em&gt;maker&lt;/em&gt; who focuses on action and the &lt;em&gt;process&lt;/em&gt; of doing something and doesn't overthink too much. The "just do it" attitude.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To someone who always wants to keep their notes clean and puts covers on their books and notebooks, this is very appealing. It's an "opposites attract" kind of situation: Because I'm the type of person who wants every page of the notebook to "look good" and gets bummed out when they "ruin a page" with a bad drawing, I admire people who can just put something on the page and move on. I think I often end up holding myself back, limiting my options and potential, because I care about form and doing things properly so much. If I spent more time trying, failing, and learning while doing, I'd probably get to where I want to be faster.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So in a way, this photo serves as a reminder to myself to &lt;em&gt;focus more on action and process.&lt;/em&gt; To treat my tools a bit more roughly - not in a "move fast and break things" kind of way, but just a &lt;em&gt;bit&lt;/em&gt; more worry-free. They're tools, they're meant to be used, not pampered. Yes, my notebooks and pens might get scratches, I'll make mistakes, and create a lot of bad drawings. But if that gets me where I want to go, it'll be worth it, and the traces left on the tools will let them develop their very own charm over time. It's not just old, kintsugi'd tea cups and antique wooden furniture that can embody beauty in imperfection. Beat-up pens or messy notebooks can, too.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/focusing-on-the-process-and-casual-wabi-sabi/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-24T13:30:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>

    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I paid for a lifetime subscription to Bear after discovering that this is a better place to spend my time scrolling. Thanks to &lt;a href='https://github.com/kagisearch/smallweb'&gt;Kagi Small Web&lt;/a&gt; for the introduction.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I do not have much of a plan here yet. I just want a simple place to write things down, collect and work through ideas, and keep a public trail of what I am learning.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Some posts will be technical. Some will be half-formed. Some will probably just be notes to myself. That sounds fine.&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>https://rnotte.art/turning-your-brain-off/</id>
    <title>turning your brain off</title>
    <updated>2026-04-23T21:49:17.124565+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>rnotte</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;ever since the COVID-19 pandemic, it seems a certain group of people who spend way too much time on the internet have adapted a principle of &lt;strong&gt;"turning your brain off"&lt;/strong&gt;. don't think, just consume.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i mean, i get why. i get why you'd want to scroll through tik tok 2 hours a day. i get why you'd want to indulge on junk food. i get why you'd want to go on temu and buy a haul of stuff you don't need. i get why you'd want to watch an anime about an average joe in a JRPG-esque fantasy world getting super OP skills and a bunch of hot girls who all want to &lt;em&gt;[REDACTED]&lt;/em&gt; him. life is frustrating, and sometimes you just want to melt your brain and numb yourself to it all. i get that, i really do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;if anything, &lt;strong&gt;that just makes me hate it even more.&lt;/strong&gt; i can't help but believe that the rich men want us to follow this principle, because it's a distraction from more important issues. issues that they, the rich men, caused. don't get it twisted; this is all &lt;em&gt;their&lt;/em&gt; fault.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;we can sit here on our computers and type out condescending comments against folks who spend too much time on social media, telling them to "touch grass". but i'm not going to do that. it's not helpful. instead, if you are one of those folks, and you're reading this, i have a question for you.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;why?&lt;/strong&gt; why do you indulge in social media, fast food, temu/aliexpress/wish/shein, and wish-fulfillment fiction, while still complaining about how bad it is? it's not healthy. it's an unhealthy addiction, just like gambling or drugs. and i have a proposal to help you break free from it:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;mark down a week on your calendar. throughout that week, uninstall your social media apps. plan to take a walk or bike ride (if you have a bike) once a day. if there's something you've been wanting to do for a while, such as reading a book or working on a project, do it. think of a skill you'd like to learn, and take time to learn it. take a piece of paper, and write down how you're feeling each day. the first step is always the hardest, but you will see that it's worth it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;and whenever you choose to do this, good luck. &lt;strong&gt;i believe in you.&lt;/strong&gt; sincerely.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://rnotte.art/turning-your-brain-off/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-23T21:49:17.124565+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://notes.jeddacp.com/on-making-and-breaking-routines/</id>
    <title>On Making and Breaking Routines</title>
    <updated>2026-04-23T21:23:16.099128+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>jedda</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;h3 id=it-takes-21-days-to-form-a-habit&gt;It takes 21 days to form a habit.&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;I used to think that I could build a routine, and keep it as long as I was disciplined enough. There is comfort in that mindset, in believing that as long as we find something that works, we can hold on to it and it’s one less stressor in life.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;I was wrong.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Routines are not fixed. They shift because &lt;em&gt;we&lt;/em&gt; shift. They depend on circumstances, energy, and the version of ourselves that exists in a particular moment.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When a routine is in place, life feels a little calmer. There is less decision-making that needs to be done, less friction. Small actions repeat until they become almost second nature, and even things that used to be difficult are &lt;em&gt;at least&lt;/em&gt; manageable. That sense of rhythm can make everything else feel more grounded, and more in control.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think about that when it comes to early mornings. There was a time when waking up before the sun, even as someone who is &lt;a href='/i-am-not-a-morning-person/'&gt;not a morning person&lt;/a&gt;, became my norm. It was not easy (I still complained a lot), but it was consistent enough that it stopped feeling like I was going to crash out. It was just something I &lt;em&gt;did&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=then-life-changed-and-so-that-routine-went-into-the-trash&gt;Then life changed, and so that routine went into the trash.&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;When my days no longer &lt;em&gt;needed&lt;/em&gt; me to wake up early, I let that structure go and built something that was more &lt;em&gt;me&lt;/em&gt;, as a non-morning person. Slower (later-ish) mornings were made for that time in my life. But returning to early mornings &lt;em&gt;now&lt;/em&gt; feels harder than expected. I hate being reminded that just because something felt natural before does not mean it will feel that way again.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That same pattern shows up in other aspects of my life too. Writing blog posts, for example, is something that benefits from a steady rhythm. When I had that in previous years, it felt easier to show up and publish consistently. Once that cadence broke, getting back into it requires more effort than I expected, even though my desire to write has never left.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Journaling for myself is &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; the same. It used to be part of my daily routine, something I did without much thought. I would wake up, drink coffee, and journal. Nowadays, I fall behind and have to catch up later, which changes how it &lt;em&gt;feels&lt;/em&gt;. It’s become something I need to manage instead of something that just fits in my day.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I don’t even know how this train of thought started, but it got me thinking that routines are less permanent than I thought they were &lt;em&gt;supposed&lt;/em&gt; to be. They are tied to specific parts of our lives, and when those parts change, the routines often do too.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There is a tendency to see a broken routine as something to fix, to try to return to what once worked. Returning is not always simple. Instead, it’s better to just find something else that fits into who we are now, not who we were when that routine first took shape. And so that's what I'm &lt;em&gt;attempting&lt;/em&gt; to do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’m in the process of rebuilding routines that fit me &lt;em&gt;now&lt;/em&gt;, rather than forcefully recreating something that worked for early-2025 me. I think I’m just trying to accept that there will be times when things feel less structured, and that this does not mean I am off track.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=this-new-rhythm-is-honestly-throwing-me-off-my-rhythm-but-im-working-on-it&gt;This new rhythm is honestly throwing me off my rhythm, but I’m working on it.&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;TBD on if I'm successful or not, or if I revert back to myself from &lt;em&gt;the before times&lt;/em&gt; -- whoever that may have been.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;details open&gt;
&lt;summary&gt;Comments&lt;/summary&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If you'd like to comment, please send me an email, or sign my &lt;a href='/guestbook/'&gt;Guestbook&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/details&gt;
&lt;h5 id=a-hrefmailtoheyjeddacpmereply-by-emaila&gt;&lt;a href='mailto:hey@jeddacp.me'&gt;Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h5&gt;</content>

    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Hey everyone! Thanks again for checking out &lt;a href='https://bearroll.dev'&gt;bearroll.dev&lt;/a&gt;, the daily roll of Bear Blog's top posts. The support has been much appreciated :)&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'm here to share a tip for those wanting to read bear blog trending posts with less distractions in a dedicated mobile app view.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You can do this is through adding Bear Roll to your home screen.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=iphone-instructions&gt;iPhone Instructions&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;ol&gt;

&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/bearroll/share-button-1.webp" alt="share-button" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ol start="3"&gt;

&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/bearroll/add-to-homescreen-2.webp" alt="add-to-homescreen" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ol start="4"&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Tap "Add" in the top right corner.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/bearroll/final-add-1.webp" alt="final-add" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=android-instructions&gt;Android Instructions&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I don't own an Android device but based on &lt;a href='https://www.wikihow.com/Set-a-Bookmark-Shortcut-in-Your-Home-Screen-on-Android'&gt;this WikiHow article&lt;/a&gt; the instructions are: go to &lt;a href='https://bearroll.dev'&gt;bearroll.dev&lt;/a&gt; on Chrome, click the three dot options icon in the top right, then click "Add to Home Screen".&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=all-done&gt;All done!&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;After you've done this you will have a Bear icon 🐻 on your device home screen. When entering the website this way you get a focused experience with no search bar or extra buttons. Just bear blogs trending posts in a chronological view.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Hope this helps!&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>https://mason.bearblog.dev/make-private-media/</id>
    <title>make private media</title>
    <updated>2026-04-23T20:57:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>mason</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Sometimes I am quite annoyed that I have lived my entire life in a digital age. Everyone around me has their heads in their screen. I can't really say much, I spend just as long on my computer each day as some of my friends spend on tik too. If I am bothering to ratify that then most of my time on my computer is productive and the leisure I do get from it is healthier than watching tik toks(it should be noted that technology can be used for leisure and productivity simultaneously, eg: blogging). But I don't actually want to ratify it today.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;20 years ago, I assume that most people didn't carry around video cameras that connected to the internet and broadcasted their view to strangers on the internet. But something I have actually seem in movies is "home videos/movies". So before we all had internet machines in our pockets, it was still normalised to film you family and loved ones? Not for broadcast but for the sake of private media.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think this is a wonderful idea, while I dont have experience with home videos because well, &lt;em&gt;"there's a camera on your phone why would you ever need to buy a seperste camera"&lt;/em&gt;, said the mother of the photographer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If someone in my family has ever gone to take a photo of me or us, they would say &lt;em&gt;"smiiiiilleeeee"&lt;/em&gt;. Thats performance, and when I think about it I dont know if the thing to do to capture memories is to put on a performance rather than carry a digicam in your pocket and occasionally capture memories of you and your friends or family in the moment.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Similarly to Hermans &lt;a href='https://herman.bearblog.dev/the-commodification-of-travel/'&gt;Commodification of travel&lt;/a&gt; , you cannot &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; a place and you cannot &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; a moment. Especially not while performing for an internet box that will gamble a photo of you on the attention economy.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I am going to try and find a digicam at an op shop and I am going to start making home videos for and of my family. Make private media, not for performance but for yourself.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://mason.bearblog.dev/make-private-media/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-23T20:57:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://tadaima.bearblog.dev/just-some-boring-advice-on-consistency/</id>
    <title>Just some boring advice on consistency</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T22:06:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>tadaima</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Being consistent and sticking with a routine is something I only seriously started doing like a year ago. For most of my life I would start things with insane enthusiasm, to the point that it would take up all my time and mental space. Then I would quickly burn out, grow bored, and then abandon whatever it was I was obsessed with.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The mainstream advice when it comes to productivity and consistency is always the same: come up with a routine and stick with it until it becomes a habit. Procrastination is just resistance, and resistance is just fear, and fear is just our stupid brain thinking there's danger where there is none. The only way to break the cycle is to teach your brain that stress is not the same as fear, and you do that by completing tasks. Like an overbearing parent, once your brain sees you can actually do things, it starts to trust us more and stops making us feel anxious about everything.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I know this, everyone knows this, but &lt;em&gt;I still hate routine&lt;/em&gt;. I hate being forced to do things when I don't feel like doing them. So I came up with my own system.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Since I'm good at having big, explosive amounts of energy followed by weeks of burnout, I use it to my advantage. Take this blog for example. I was pretty inconsistent at first, but then found a way to stay productive. Instead of writing posts here and there then feeling completely over it, I now batch-write several posts at once whenever that burst of energy hits. I leave all the posts in draft and just let them sit there. Then, once a week, I go in and publish whatever draft that makes the most sense and looks the least sloppy. Easy peasy.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Any time I'm not consistent, it's usually because I procrastinated and let the cache go empty and now I have to find the time to refill it.&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have a similar system with other writing projects. During bouts of energy I'll write a ton without stopping, without sticking to a particular goal. Then, during burn-out days, I'll only write a little, like incoherent/stream of conscious-type stuff that doesn't take too much energy.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It even extends to reading. I have a goal of reading 2-4 books a month, which I have stuck to even though I don't always read every day. Sometimes I'll read a quarter of a novel over two weeks and then finish the rest of the book in one night. Even though I do it a bit differently, it's all still a routine at the end of the day.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Routine and consistency. It's boring, but it works.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;Like today. 👀&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://tadaima.bearblog.dev/just-some-boring-advice-on-consistency/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-04-24T22:06:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>

    <title>ʕ•ᴥ•ʔﾉﾞ pinewind: a chill bearblog</title>

    <author>
      <name>ohmyblog</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;div align="center"&gt;&lt;a href="https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/"&gt;&lt;img class="pixel-bear" src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/ohmyblog/image-2.webp"&gt;&lt;/img&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;pinewind, a blog by kwist, gives us a calm space to enjoy the jots and thoughts of a highly interesting Japan-based hobbyist, enthusiast, and multipotentialite writer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i can't decide if my favorite post is his &lt;a href='https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/thought-log-blogging/' target='_blank'&gt;thought-log on blogging&lt;/a&gt; or his post on &lt;a href='https://pinewind.bearblog.dev/thought-log-blogging' target='_blank'&gt;personal colour pallets&lt;/a&gt;. both posts show the breadth of kwist's interests.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;he considers his blog more of a garden. i have certainly appreciated wandering through his garden and have secretly (not anymore) taken some cuttings home with me to graft onto my own projects. please take a patient wander through pinewind, you will experience a lovely visit:&lt;/p&gt;
